title: Greet Phoebe (Romans 16)
hookLine: the letter ends with a list of people, many of them women, like Phoebe the deacon

lines: THE FIRST NAME: A WOMAN WITH THE LETTER.
cards: Chapter sixteen of Romans looks like the credits at the end of a movie: a long list of names nobody can pronounce. Greet this one. Greet that one.
Salute the household of so-and-so. Most people skip it. But stay for the credits: some of the best stories in the letter hide in that list.
The very first name belongs to a woman traveling from a port town near Corinth, probably with the letter itself in her bag.

teach.b: Paul writes, in the King James Bible: "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea." Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth. Servant here is diakonos, the root of deacon.
Paul uses the same word for himself as a minister of the gospel, and even for Christ.
Many scholars think Phoebe carried this letter to Rome, so she may have been the first to read it aloud there and answer questions about it.
Paul asks the Romans to help her in whatever she needs, and calls her a helper, a patron, of many, and of Paul himself. Then the list.
Priscilla and Aquila, a wife and husband who, Paul says, risked their necks for him, and who host a church in their home. Mary, who worked hard.
Andronicus and Junia, who were in prison with Paul, and whom he calls of note among the apostles. Tryphaena and Tryphosa, two women who labor in the Lord.
Rufus's mother, who, Paul says, was a mother to him too. More than two dozen names, around a third of them women.

teach.h: I TERTIUS, WHO WROTE THIS EPISTLE.
teach.b: Even the secretary pops up: I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you. Churches today differ on women's roles.

teach.h: I COMMEND UNTO YOU PHEBE OUR SISTER.
teach.b: Many Protestant churches ordain women as deacons, and some as pastors. The early churches of the East had deaconesses, and some Orthodox churches are discussing restoring them.
The Catholic Church ordains only men as deacons, and has been studying the question. But every church can read this list the same way: every name was a real someone.

how: Many churches remember Phoebe, Priscilla and Junia among the saints and early leaders, and in most traditions deacons serve the poor, help in worship and care for the practical life of the congregation.

o: a church elder chosen to settle disputes
a senior priest who leads a whole region
a servant or minister who serves the church

games.q: who's in the list — tap the pairs.
p: a diakonos who likely carried the letter

s: Romans 16 is just a list of names with no stories
Phoebe, Priscilla, Junia, Rufus's mother and the scribe Tertius all appear with a detail or a story.
the word for Phoebe's role is the same one we get deacon from
diakonos, a word Paul also uses for himself and for Christ.
all churches agree on whether women can be ordained deacons
many Protestant churches do, some Orthodox churches are discussing restoring deaconesses, and the Catholic Church ordains only men.

games.q: you're Paul, finishing your greatest letter. who do you name first?
o: the leading men of the Roman church.
games.why: "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea." she was probably the one carrying the letter.

practice: Think of the people who keep a place of faith or care running, whose names rarely get said: the person who sets up chairs, the one who runs the food pantry, a choir director, a janitor, a nursery volunteer, a chaplain; if you don't belong to a church, anyone who serves quietly, like a school secretary, a nurse or a crossing guard.
Pick one and say their name to yourself, the way Paul does: greet this one. If you pray, give thanks for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Deacon. Diakonos in Greek: a servant, a minister. And Phoebe of Cenchreae, the first name in Paul's closing list, carries it.

orig.note: Greek: servant, minister, deacon. used of Phoebe, of Paul, and of Christ.

carryVoice: Your line: every name is someone. That's the end of Romans. Tomorrow, the lookout over the year.
